events.title: Fort Fisher
events.text: An L of sand at the tip of Federal Point, guarding New Inlet and the blockade-runners' road to Wilmington. The land face runs some 1,300 feet from the river to the Northeast Bastion: a parapet 25 feet thick with twenty-odd guns in barbette among fifteen traverses, each a bombproof, a palisade in front and torpedo wires beyond it. The sea face runs two-thirds of a mile down the beach to the Mound Battery; a mile of sand plain separates that from Battery Buchanan at the point. Colonel William Lamb built it and commands it.

events.title: Christmas 1864
events.text: Three weeks earlier Butler and Porter tried it. A powder ship was blown up off the fort at 1:40 on the morning of 24 December without effect; 64 warships fired some 10,000 rounds that day and as many on Christmas Day. Curtis landed three miles north with 500 men, and 250 of the 142nd New York came within 75 yards of Shepherd's Battery, where Lieutenant Walling took a flag. Butler called it off at dark, and Curtis and 600 men were left on the beach until the 27th.

events.title: The fleet returns
events.text: At twenty past seven on 13 January the gunboats open on the peninsula four miles north, and the second bombardment begins. Porter has 58 warships and 627 guns; five ironclads close in on the land face, the wooden lines beyond them. Terry's provisional corps, 9,632 men on the returns, is in the transports.

events.title: The landing
events.text: At eight the landing begins near Myrtle Sound, beyond the north edge of this sheet, and is not opposed; Hoke's division, about 6,400 at Sugar Loaf, does not attack. The fleet fires all day. Inside the fort Lamb has about 850 men, and 700 more come in during the day.

events.title: South toward the fort
events.text: At five Terry moves south with Paine's two brigades of U.S. Colored Troops and two of Ames's. Between two and eight next morning a line is dug across the peninsula from Battery Anderson to the river, two miles north of the fort, and Paine holds it facing Hoke. By Terry's count 4,700 stay on that line and 3,300 are for the fort.

events.title: Battery Holland
events.text: Late on the 14th Terry and Comstock go forward to Battery Holland, 500 yards north of the fort, and Porter agrees to the plan: the army on the western salient, a column of sailors and marines on the bastion. By nightfall most of the land-face guns are in ruins.

events.title: Hagood's men
events.text: Before dawn on the 15th the 21st South Carolina lands at Battery Buchanan from the river. Of about 1,000 of Hagood's brigade sent, 350 reach the fort; the 11th and 25th come across the sand plain at half past two under the fleet's fire. With them the garrison is about 1,900.

events.title: The last bombardment
events.text: From eight the fleet fires on the land face alone; by noon all but two 8-inch columbiads there are silenced. Terry is at Battery Holland by midday. The naval column lands on the beach north of the fort and works forward in trenches.

events.title: Three hundred yards
events.text: By two the sharpshooters of the 13th Indiana are within 175 yards of the western salient and Curtis's brigade is deployed 300 yards north of the fort, Pennypacker and Bell behind it. The 11th and 25th South Carolina are still coming up the sea face from Buchanan under the fleet's fire.

events.title: The signal
events.text: At three precisely, by Towle, Terry signals the Navy to shift its fire from the land face; the Malvern's whistle sounds at 3:25, and Terry's dispatch puts the lodgment at 3:30. The sources give three, 3:25 and 3:30 for the start. As the fire lifts Lamb puts 250 men at the western salient, 500 along the Northeast Bastion, and Hagood's 350 in a commissary bombproof.

events.title: The naval column
events.text: Two thousand sailors and marines charge the Northeast Bastion up the beach in one mass. The 500 there shoot it to a halt, about 500 yards out by some accounts, and it breaks and runs back along the beach. The Navy loses 393 men here.

events.title: The western salient
events.text: About a hundred axemen cut the palisade and Curtis's brigade goes over the parapet at Shepherd's Battery; the 117th New York's colours go up on it. The fight for the traverses begins.

events.title: The river gate
events.text: Pennypacker's brigade overlaps Curtis's right. The 203rd Pennsylvania breaks the sandbagged river gate, the palisade is cleared to the river and some 400 prisoners are taken. About 3:45 Pennypacker is shot down planting the 97th Pennsylvania's colours on the third traverse, the fifth by Towle's count.

events.title: Bell
events.text: Bell's brigade comes over the causeway at the gate; Bell is shot crossing it. At four Whiting leads a counterattack and falls wounded at the third traverse; the Federals take the fourth. More than 4,000 Union troops are now in the western salient.

events.title: Traverse by traverse
events.text: The ironclads shell the land face ahead of the Federals, and the garrison falls back toward the bastion. At half past four Lamb is wounded and carried to the Pulpit bombproof. Reilly leads about 150 men back along the face; two-thirds fall, and the rest go to the bastion. By a quarter to five seven traverses are held.

events.title: Sunset
events.text: The sun sets at twelve past five and the fight goes on among the traverses in the dark. Curtis is wounded at half past five.

events.title: Abbott
events.text: At six Abbott's brigade, 1,494 men, comes through the river gate from Terry's line and forms inside the fort.

events.title: The last traverses
events.text: In the evening Ames turns the flank of the remaining traverses, and the last of them falls within a few minutes; nine traverses are taken in all, and the garrison abandons the bastion for the sea face and the sand plain.

events.title: Battery Buchanan
events.text: At nine Reilly carries Lamb and Whiting to Battery Buchanan, where Chapman's sailors have left by boat. At half past nine the 27th U.S. Colored Troops comes down the sea face after them; Colquitt, sent by Bragg to take command, rows away as it passes the wharf.

events.title: Surrender
events.text: About ten o'clock the garrison surrenders at Buchanan and Whiting gives up the fort to Terry: 112 officers and 1,971 men, by Terry's count. The army's official loss is 664, the Navy's 393; the Confederates lost about 500 killed and wounded and the rest captured. Next morning the main magazine blows up and kills or wounds about 200 more. Wilmington's last port is shut.

outcome.result: Union victory: the fort and its garrison taken
losses: Army, official: 664 (111 killed, 540 wounded, 13 missing), by brigade Curtis 228, Pennypacker 280, Bell 115, Abbott 31. The January table gives 1,059. Navy: 393 (88 killed, 271 wounded, 34 missing). Another 104 soldiers at least in the magazine explosion of the 16th.
About 500 killed and wounded and about 1,400 captured, 1,900 in all; Terry counted 112 officers and 1,971 men taken. Whiting mortally wounded, Lamb wounded.
outcome.note: The fleet fired 19,682 projectiles in January, 1,652,638 pounds of iron; both attacks together nearly 40,000. The sources give three, 3:25 and 3:30 for the hour of the assault.

sources: Cyrus B. Comstock, Plan and sections of Fort Fisher, carried by assault by the U.S. forces, Maj. Gen. A.H. Terry commanding, Jan. 15th, 1865 (Engineer Bureau, 1:3,840; Library of Congress 86690228), and Comstock and Schultze, Sketch of vicinity of Fort Fisher (1:12,000; LC 86690227): the traverses, the gate, the palisade, the rifle pits, the sea face and the road down the peninsula. The two sheets disagree by about 300 m on the Mound.

Fort Fisher, National Register of Historic Places nomination, Polly M. Rettig, NPS Landmark Review Project, 1975 (from Frank B. Sarles Jr., 1961): the fort as built, its guns, the palisade and torpedoes, the December attack, and what the sea has taken since.

North Carolina Historic Sites, Fort Fisher: "1st Attack", "2nd Attack" and "Casualties and Other Numbers", the clock of 13 to 16 January from Mark A. Moore, The Wilmington Campaign and the Battles for Fort Fisher (1999), with the strengths and losses from the Official Records, the naval records and Battles and Leaders.

Terry's and Ames's reports of 16 January 1865 (OR Series I, vol. 46, part 1) and Lt. Col. George F. Towle's narrative of 31 December 1865, as reprinted in Senate Report 1578, 56th Congress (1900), on Galusha Pennypacker: the hour of the signal, the lodgment, the gate and the colours on the traverses.

The orders of battle from OR I/46/1 pp. 403-405 and ORN I/11 (Porter, Breese); William Lamb, "The Defense of Fort Fisher", Battles and Leaders vol. IV; Rod Gragg, Confederate Goliath (1991); Chris Fonvielle, The Wilmington Campaign (1997). The last three not consulted directly.
Fort Fisher, captured by the Federals, Jan. 15, 1865, manuscript map from Rear Adm. David D. Porter's papers (LC 99446439): the fleet's lines of battle and the fort's range arcs.

Places: the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey's points for Shepherd's Battery, the Northeast Bastion and Battery Buchanan; the headquarters site under the UDC column and the modern shore from OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Terrain: USGS 3DEP elevation at 10 m over a 4 km square, with the strip the sea has taken since 1865 (the bastion, 2,100 ft of the sea face and the beach north of it) raised to beach height, and New Inlet, closed in 1881, drawn as water.

What is reconstructed: the Mound Battery's place, between Comstock's two sheets; the sea face's line and its batteries; the regimental strengths, split evenly from the brigade and division aggregates; where each regiment stood as the traverses fell; the naval column's landing place and approach; the stations of the ships on the 15th, from Porter's plan of lines rather than the day's positions; and the ships drawn as batteries on the water. Terry's line and the landing beach are beyond the north edge, so the Union columns come on there.
